# Engine hot, radiator cold

When an engine sits at operating temperature while its primary heat exchanger remains ice-cold to the touch, you are looking at a fundamental flow restriction issue rather than a simple thermostat failure. The scenario described—an Audi A3 8L1 overheating with a cold radiator—points directly to a blockage in the coolant loop or a pump that has lost its ability to move fluid against resistance.

The symptom of hot engine, cold radiator is the classic signature of a blocked upper hose or a collapsed core. In many cooling systems, air pockets can migrate to the highest point, often near the thermostat housing or the top of the radiator neck. If air locks occur here, they act as an insulator that prevents heat transfer from the coolant to the metal fins, rendering the radiator ineffective despite the coolant being at boiling point inside the engine block.

Another critical component to evaluate is the water pump itself. The 8L1 generation often utilized a mechanical impeller driven by the timing belt or chain. If the impeller has corroded, become loose on the shaft, or failed entirely, the pump will spin without moving any fluid. You can verify this by feeling the radiator inlet hose while the engine is running; it should be hot throughout the entire drive cycle. If the top hose remains cool until the very end of a run or never heats up significantly, the coolant is not circulating through the core.

The timing belt change mentioned in the diagnosis report requires immediate attention. On many Audi platforms from this era, the water pump and tensioner were integrated into the service interval for the timing chain or belt. If the belt was replaced but the water pump bearings were overlooked, internal wear could have gone unnoticed until the engine reached normal operating temperatures. A failing bearing can cause shaft wobble, leading to impeller failure even if the external pulley looks fine.

You also dismissed the heater core clog, which is a logical deduction since the cabin vents are blowing hot air. The heater core draws from the same coolant loop as the radiator; however, because it is located inside the car (lower in the chassis), gravity and pressure dynamics sometimes allow flow to persist even when the main radiator circuit is partially starved. That said, if the heater core were severely clogged on the outlet side, you might see reduced airflow or a temperature drop at the vents once the engine hits 90°C. Since the heat remains consistent there, the blockage is almost certainly upstream in the radiator inlet or the upper hose connection.

To isolate the issue without disassembly immediately, perform a pressure test on the cooling system while it is cold. A standard mechanic's gauge can reveal if the system holds pressure; a drop indicates an external leak, but sometimes internal leaks into the combustion chamber (head gasket) can also confuse the picture by introducing air bubbles that mimic blockages. If the system holds pressure and hoses are intact, you may need to flush the radiator with distilled water and a flush chemical additive designed to dissolve sludge common in older VW/Audi platforms.

Sometimes the issue isn't a broken part but a configuration error during the thermostat replacement. While reversing the thermostat is unlikely given the visual symmetry of most modern units, failing to bleed the air from the system after installation is a frequent oversight. The 8L1 engine bay can be tricky for air pockets to escape naturally if the fill cap isn't opened properly or if the expansion tank wasn't cycled correctly.

If flushing and bleeding do not restore flow, the radiator itself may have internal corrosion blocking the core passages. At that point, replacement is often more cost-effective than cleaning unless you have access to a specialized ultrasonic cleaner capable of removing heavy sediment from aluminum cores. Always replace the upper hose as well, as aging rubber combined with high coolant temperatures can lead to microscopic cracks that collapse under vacuum conditions when the engine cools down.
